title: Why Java's AOT cache feels like a free startup boost with hidden risks
excerpt: The new AOT cache can cut startup time, but incompatibilities and crashes make it a fragile feature for real-world apps.
body:
A recent rollout at XPipe showed that the JDK’s AOT cache can shave seconds off startup without any code changes, but only when the JVM actually loads the cache. In the best case the cache is ignored because of incompatibilities; in the worst case the JVM crashes during launch.

The following sections explain how the cache is built on top of class-data sharing, what conditions cause it to be skipped or to explode, and how to generate a reliable cache for a production build.

## How the AOT cache is built on class-data sharing  

Class-data sharing (CDS) has been part of HotSpot since JDK 5. It writes parsed class metadata into a shared archive that the JVM maps directly into memory at startup. Over the years CDS gained application-level sharing (JDK 10), a default JDK-class archive (JDK 12) and dynamic archives (JDK 13). The AOT cache reuses this same infrastructure, which is why logs still contain the “cds” tag and the archive is often called a “shared archive”.

When an application runs with `-XX:+AOTClassLinking`, the JVM records which classes are loaded, linked and which methods are invoked. The recorded data is then written to an AOT cache file. The file can hold several kinds of information:

* Loaded class data, the same bytes that CDS stores.  
* Method profiles, call-site frequencies that help the JIT warm up faster (added in JDK 25).  
* Cached Java objects, usable with any GC starting in JDK 26.  
* Pre-linked classes, classes are stored already linked so the JVM can skip that step on the next launch.

The cache itself is just a file; the JVM reads it on subsequent starts and skips the corresponding initialization work. Because the underlying mechanism is identical to CDS, the same command-line switches that control CDS (for example `-Xshare:off`) also affect the AOT cache.

## Pitfalls that can cause the cache to be ignored or crash the JVM  

The feature is still rough around the edges. XPipe’s experience highlighted three common failure modes.

1. Incompatible JVM options, Flags that disable CDS, such as `-Xshare:off`, also prevent the AOT cache from being loaded. The JVM silently falls back to a cold start, so the expected boost never appears.  
2. Missing class-linking flag, The cache contains pre-linked classes only when `-XX:+AOTClassLinking` is enabled during creation. If the flag is omitted, the cache still exists but the JVM cannot use the linking optimization, reducing the benefit dramatically.  
3. Crash on cache load, Certain combinations of GC, JIT settings, or native libraries cause the JVM to segfault while mapping the archive. XPipe observed crashes when using a custom GC together with an older JDK 24 build that lacked the object-caching extension introduced in JDK 26. The crash is hard to diagnose because the JVM prints only a generic “Failed to map AOT cache” message.

Other subtle issues include version mismatches (the cache format changes with each JDK release) and dynamic class loading that was not exercised during the training run. If a class appears only at runtime, the JVM falls back to normal loading, which can negate the startup gain.

## Practical steps to create a reliable AOT cache for your application  

The following checklist turned XPipe’s flaky attempts into a reproducible build pipeline.

1. Use a single-step cache creation command, Starting with JDK 25 the ergonomics were simplified. The cache can be generated in one go with  

   ```
   java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot -XX:+AOTClassLinking -jar myapp.jar
   ```  

   This command records class loading, links the classes and writes method profiles into `app.aot`. The flag `-XX:AOTCacheOutput` is the only required addition; the other two flags are recommended to ensure linking and profiling are captured.

2. Run the training execution on a clean JVM, Launch the application with the same JVM options that will be used in production, except for the cache output flag. Avoid any debugging or profiling agents that could alter class loading order.

3. Validate the cache before distribution, Start the application with `-XX:AOTCacheInput=app.aot` and check the log for the “cds” tag indicating a successful load. A quick sanity check is to compare startup time with and without the `-XX:AOTCacheInput` flag; a noticeable reduction confirms that the cache is being applied.

4. Pin the JDK version, Because the cache format evolves, ship the exact JDK version that produced the cache. If you need to upgrade, regenerate the cache with the new JDK and test all target platforms.

5. Guard against GC incompatibilities, If the application uses a non-default GC, verify that the JDK version supports object caching (JDK 26 or later). For older releases, either switch to the default GC for the cache-enabled builds or disable object caching with `-XX:-AOTObjectCaching`.

6. Monitor for unexpected class loads, Enable the `-XX:+PrintAOTStats` flag in production to log any classes that were not found in the cache. Frequent misses suggest that the training run did not cover a code path that users trigger, and a new training run may be required.

By following these steps, the cache becomes a deterministic part of the launch sequence rather than an optional bonus that may disappear or crash the JVM.

## The takeaway  

The AOT cache builds on the proven CDS infrastructure, so it can provide a free startup boost when the JVM successfully maps the archive. However, incompatible flags, missing linking options, or version mismatches can cause the cache to be ignored or crash the JVM. Generate the cache in a single step with `-XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot`, keep the JVM options consistent, and verify the load on each release to turn the feature into a reliable part of the deployment pipeline.
